This is Garudan Thookkam. Ancient/Living Tradition.
on_screen: Title card: Garudan Thookkam · India · Ancient/Living Tradition

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originates from the mythological pacification of the goddess Kali.
Legend states that after slaying the demon Darika, Kali remained insatiable.
Vishnu sent Garuda to quench her thirst with his blood.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is performed as a 'votive offering' or reward for problems solved by the goddess Kali.
Key occasions include the festivals of Meena Bharani, Pathamudayam, and Makara Bharani.
It is a ritual of sacrifice and devotion intended to satisfy the family deity, Bhadrakali.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Folk Dance of Kerala (Vol. IV) (https://archive.org/details/dni.ncaa.IGNCA-36-VHS)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers dress as Garuda and engage in a night-long dance.
The movement mimics the flight of the divine eagle.
The climax involves 'Choondakuthal,' where the skin of the back is pierced with metal hooks.
Watch for Choondakuthal, Eagle Flight.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Processions on bullock carts, boats, or hand-pulled carts; three circuits around the temple
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The performance is accompanied by 'scores of chenda experts.' The chenda, a traditional cylindrical percussion instrument of Kerala, provides the rhythmic foundation for the night-long dance and the subsequent procession.
Listen for the Chenda.
The soundscape is dominated by the powerful, sharp cracks and rolling thuds of multiple chenda drums playing in unison, creating a high-energy, percussive environment that lasts throughout the night.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear elaborate costumes to resemble the divine eagle Garuda.
The setting varies from temple grounds to 'thoni vallams' (large country boats) on rivers like the Moovattupuzha, or chariot-like structures on roads.
Illuminated three-storied wooden structures called Attuvela often accompany the water-based processions.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While individual dancers are not named in the sources, the Arayankavu Bhagavathy temple is noted for holding the world record for the largest performance of the ritual.
In Vaikom, the ritual involves floating structures on boats.
The dance is a subclass of ceremonial and sacred Hindu dances in India.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Garudan Thookkam is sibling of Mayilpeeli Thookkam: Another 'Thookkam' (hanging) ritual dance variant in Kerala.
Garudan Thookkam is influence of Kathakali: Shares regional aesthetic and elaborate costuming traditions of Kerala.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: This is a blood-offering ritual involving physical piercing (Choondakuthal). Outsiders should maintain a respectful distance and observe local temple protocols regarding photography and proximity to the suspended performers.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: Witness the extreme devotion of Kerala's Garudan Thookkam, where dancers become divine birds suspended by hooks to appease a thirsty goddess.
